summary:
Van is a province of Turkey and stands under the national framework: the Turkish penal code, migration rules, health regulations and prison administration apply here in full. No trans-specific statute, enforcement pattern or incident documentation exists for Van itself, and that absence is recorded as absence of documented divergence rather than as local permissiveness.

A leaked omnibus draft identified by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025 as the "11th Judicial Package" would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with up to three years in prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, conditioned on mandatory permanent infertility assessment and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, and patients up to three years, with pretrial detention possible. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft; Human Rights Watch warns it would force treatment underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest. The measure had not been enacted as reported, but authorities have applied its prohibitions as though already in force.

Kaos GL's 2025 national monitoring, "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", records hostility toward LGBTI+ people as explicit state policy: "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions, the closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation for the first time in years, restrictions on expression and artistic freedom, and events cancelled or banned. The same review documents six right-to-life violations including three hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected; 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the previous year; 313 liberty violations, roughly two and a half times the prior year, carrying 299 detention decisions; private-life violations rising from 16 to 67, among them obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy; and 61 travel bans.

Two parent-layer rules bear directly on a visitor in Van. Foreign nationals are required to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints country-wide, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance, so any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents are compared against presentation. Police stops for background checks have been used against trans women in public spaces in Istanbul in 2025, with detainees documented even where no fine was imposed.

Care and custody conditions are tightening at the same time. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 barred hospitals from recording the "other" option on reports and required electronic reports to be issued, a change that risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care. Trans prisoners are placed according to registered sex: a trans man had been held in a women's prison, and the death of a transgender prisoner at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025 prompted demands from rights groups for an independent investigation, with accounts of delayed medical response, prosecutors entering two days later, and witnesses not interviewed. The case was raised in parliament on 12 December 2025.
tangentialFactors:
Van's status as a province with no locally documented incidents makes it an illustration of the national pattern rather than an exception to it. The provincial record carries the country-level regime unchanged: the draft criminalising package, the monitoring totals, the identification checkpoints and the prison placement rules all reach Van through the same statutory and administrative channels that apply in Istanbul or Ankara.

The 61 travel bans recorded by Kaos GL for 2025 are the most directly transit-adjacent figure in the inventory. They indicate that movement restrictions are being used as a measured instrument against LGBT people, which is relevant to anyone planning cross-border routing through a province that sits on an international frontier.

The relationship between drafting and enforcement is asymmetric. The 11th Judicial Package remained a draft as of its October 2025 reporting, yet trans women stopped by police in 2025 stated that officers applied the new law's logic before any statute had been passed. The gap between a measure's legislative status and its street-level effect is therefore not a reliable safety margin.

Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need for a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's depth, not as a statement of current law.
localsOnly:
Residents of Van live under the same monitoring environment recorded nationally by Kaos GL. Public institutions received "Year of the Family" instructions, an LGBTI+ rights organisation was closed for the first time in years, artistic and expressive activity was restricted, and events were cancelled or banned during 2025.

Private-life violations affecting residents rose from 16 to 67 over the year, a category that includes obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy. The September 2025 Health Ministry regulation requiring electronic reports and barring the "other" option alters how transition-related care is recorded in official medical systems, and a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular had added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports.

Custody for residents is governed by registered sex and by isolation practices rather than gender-matched placement. Prison conditions documented country-wide include arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, refusals of hospital transfer, no staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, binary administrative practice, transfers that disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints processes that are ineffective and can attract further violence.

The 2025 totals against LGBT people reached 313 liberty violations with 299 detention decisions, 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, six right-to-life violations including three hate-motivated killings, and 61 travel bans. Private organising in Van therefore operates under a documented escalation rather than an ordinary baseline.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory documents any incident, arrest, prosecution, Pride event, police action, clinic refusal or court case inside Van province. Whether enforcement diverges from the national pattern in either direction is unresolved and not sourced here.

The enactment status of the 11th Judicial Package is unresolved. It was reported as a leaked draft on 29 October 2025 with opposition from fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association; no source in this inventory confirms whether it has been passed, amended or withdrawn since.

It is not sourced whether the Kaos GL 2025 counts include any incident occurring in Van, since the report is compiled at national level without a provincial breakdown in this inventory.

The outcome of the Sincan Women's Prison death investigation raised in parliament on 12 December 2025, and of the demanded independent inquiry, is unresolved in these sources.
